name: Vangrd.bot
tagline: A hosted service for running unattended bots and scheduled automations without maintaining your own box.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Public detail on this one is thin, so read this as a ruling on the shape of the thing: hosted bots that run on a schedule and act on your behalf. The logic inside any single bot is small, and a coding agent will write it plus a scheduler in an afternoon. What you are actually paying for is the part that runs at 3am without you: retries, rate limit backoff, credential handling, and an alert when a job quietly stops doing anything. That is buildable, but it is a weekend followed by a permanent tax every time an upstream API shifts under you. Worth doing if you own one or two automations and do not mind being the on-call engineer.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted job runner that executes your bot scripts on a cron schedule, keeps state in SQLite, retries on failure, and pings a webhook when a run breaks or goes silent.
requirements: An always-on machine or cheap VPS, since cron on a laptop is not cron
API keys or tokens for whatever the bot actually touches, in .env
A notification sink you already read, Slack or Telegram or plain email
whatYouLose: Someone else's uptime, so your automation dies quietly when your VPS reboots
Prebuilt connectors and templates, you write every integration by hand
A real dashboard with run history, logs and diffs instead of grepping a SQLite file
Maintenance when upstream APIs change shape, which they will
QA discipline: a bot that runs but does the wrong thing is worse than one that crashes
moatNotes: Not a data or network moat, just the unglamorous work of keeping unattended jobs correct and visible over months.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because writing a bot is a Saturday and operating one is forever. The failure mode of DIY automation is not a stack trace, it is six weeks of silence where you assumed something was running and it was not. Paying for a hosted runner buys observability, alerting and a maintenance culture you would otherwise have to invent for yourself, and for anything touching money, customers or credentials that is a rational trade.
notes: Bot logic is cheap, bot reliability is not.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted bot runner I can deploy on a single small VPS. No accounts, no multi-tenancy, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: TypeScript on Node 20, better-sqlite3 for storage, node-cron for scheduling, Hono for a tiny local HTTP dashboard, Vitest for tests. No Docker orchestration, a single process is fine.

Core behaviour:
1. Bots live in ./bots as .ts files. Each exports a default object: { id, schedule (cron string), timeoutMs, run(ctx) }.
2. ctx gives the bot: a logger, a get/set key-value store scoped to that bot id, and a fetch wrapper with timeout and exponential backoff on 429 and 5xx.
3. On boot, load every bot, validate the schedule, register it with node-cron, and print a table of what will run when.
4. Every run is recorded in SQLite: bot id, start, end, status (ok, error, timeout), attempt count, log lines, and a short result string the bot may return.
5. Retries: up to 3 attempts with jittered backoff. After the final failure, write the run as error and fire an alert.
6. Heartbeat watchdog: if a bot has not completed a successful run within 2x its expected interval, fire a stale alert once, then suppress until it recovers.
7. Alerts go to a generic webhook URL from .env (Slack and Telegram incoming webhooks both work). If the URL is missing, log loudly instead of crashing.
8. Dashboard on localhost:8787: list of bots with last run status and next run time, a run detail page with logs, and a POST endpoint to trigger a bot manually.
9. Secrets only from .env via a typed config module that fails fast on missing required keys. Never log secret values.
10. Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop scheduling, let in-flight runs finish up to 30 seconds, then exit.

Also include: a dry-run mode that executes a single bot once and exits with a non-zero code on failure, so I can test in CI.

Ship two example bots: one that hits a public JSON endpoint and stores a value, and one that deliberately fails so I can see retries, alerts and the error page working.

Out of scope: user auth, hosted UI, plugin marketplace, LLM agents, queues beyond SQLite, anything distributed.

Write a README with setup, a systemd unit file, and one paragraph on how to add a new bot.
